learningObjective: Distinguish eager execution (define-by-run) from static graph capture (define-and-run) and identify the correct implications of each.

canonicalClaims.claim: The essential difference between eager and static execution is whether a persistent computation graph is constructed before execution: eager dispatches operations immediately, while static capture builds an IR that later passes can optimize globally.
conditions: The framework's default mode is being described (not overrides).
The comparison is at the graph representation level.
nonImplications: Does not imply eager frameworks cannot compile subgraphs (torch.compile does).
Does not imply that eager is always slower than compiled; overhead varies with model and hardware.

misconceptions.claim: Eager and static differ mainly in the file format of the graph.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The difference is when the graph is constructed, not the format.

misconceptions.claim: Static graph mode is always faster than eager.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Compile-time cost, dispatch overhead, and per-op efficiency all vary; eager competitive on many workloads.

misconceptions.claim: Eager mode requires a JIT compiler for every Python line.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Eager dispatches to pre-compiled kernels; no per-line JIT is required.

misconceptions.claim: Eager mode is only for debugging.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Eager is used in production workflows; it also underpins hybrid setups like torch.compile.

implementationFacts: PyTorch eager: dispatch to ATen ops; no graph captured
torch.compile: capture subgraphs from Python bytecode; compile via Inductor
TensorFlow 1.x: define-and-run (Session/Graph); TF 2.x default is eager
performanceScenarios: Compiled subgraphs enable fusion and kernel-selection wins; eager execution retains Python flexibility for control flow and iteration.
